query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, phase stability is governed by a composition‐dependent thermodynamic instability: once local Al concentrations reach a critical threshold during cooling, the resulting short-range order triggers rapid, diffusion‐mediated separation into a partially ordered B2 phase (rich in Ni, Co, and Al) and a disordered BCC matrix (rich in Cr and Fe).
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high‐temperature, disordered BCC state
generation.intervention: Perform in situ high-temperature annealing with controlled temperature ramps and hold times near the predicted threshold (around 550–650 °C), while monitoring structural evolution using diffraction techniques.
generation.conditions: The alloy is first homogenized at high temperature (>800 °C) to ensure a uniform disordered BCC state, then cooled with controlled holds spanning 550–650 °C to capture the onset of ordering. A controlled comparison is made with samples maintained above the threshold temperature (e.g., 800 °C) where no ordering occurs.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of short-range order around Al atoms leads to local compositional fluctuations that favor the formation of Ni-Co-Al enriched B2 regions, segregating from Cr-Fe rich BCC areas.
generation.mechanism: As the alloy cools, increasing local Al concentrations lower the configurational entropy advantage of the BCC state. Once the thermal activation reaches a critical point, atomic diffusion rapidly rearranges the lattice into a partially ordered B2 phase. This process is driven by the enthalpic gain from ordering (especially between Al, Ni, and Co) that overcomes kinetic barriers, resulting in a two-phase system with distinct local chemistries.
generation.predicted_outcome: A sharp increase in B2-characteristic diffraction superlattice peak intensities should be observable around 550–650 °C, accompanied by a calorimetric transition (exothermic or endothermic peak) and microstructural evidence of partitioning: Ni, Co, and Al concentrating in the ordered phase while Cr and Fe remain in the disordered matrix.
generation.baseline: A sample kept at a consistently high temperature (e.g., >800 °C) will maintain a uniform, disordered BCC state with no significant B2 phase indicators or compositional segregation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected in the narrow temperature regime where diffusion kinetics become significant (approximately 550–650 °C) and when the alloy’s composition is maintained uniform. Deviations such as excessive residence time or compositional nonuniformity may lead to secondary phase formation (e.g., sigma phase), which are outside the scope of this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: While the controlled variable approach can identify a transformation threshold, the exact critical temperature and time scale for the onset of B2 ordering may vary with minor compositional fluctuations and experimental conditions. Quantitative measures of the diffusion acceleration are also not precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples under identical high-temperature homogenization conditions. Subject samples to in situ annealing experiments with controlled temperature steps (e.g., 700 °C, 650 °C, 600 °C, 550 °C, and 500 °C) with equal hold times. Simultaneously monitor phase evolution using X-ray or neutron diffraction, DSC, and elemental mapping. A control sample maintained at 800 °C (no cooling through the threshold) will serve as the baseline.
measurements: Intensity and appearance of B2 superlattice diffraction peaks
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) traces for thermal transitions
Elemental distribution via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping to confirm Ni-Co-Al enrichment versus Cr-Fe segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no distinct change in ordering (lack of a sharp B2 peak emergence or absence of DSC peak) is observed within 550–650 °C, or if compositional mapping does not reveal the expected segregated chemistry (i.e., B2 phase rich in Ni, Co, and Al and a BCC matrix rich in Cr and Fe), then the hypothesis that local Al-induced thermodynamic instability governs the phase transformation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: All simulated systems are disordered at high temperatures but form an ordered structure as the system is cooled. The progression of structures is shown for x = 1 in Fig. 1. To demonstrate this feature more rigorously, and to quantify the development of order, plots of ηi versus temperature from Monte Carlo simulations are shown in Fig. 3, for AlxCoCrFeNi, with Al compositions ranging from x = 1 to x = 2. One significant feature of the simulations is that the ordering onset, i.e., where the HEA is cooled below the ordering temperature, Tc, involves the strong ordering of at least two, but not necessarily all, of the n > 4 TM elements. The dominant behavior on cooling is that Al segregates to one sublattice, with Ni and Co primarily occupying the other sublattice. All behaviors are quantitatively reproduced on both heating and cooling simulations, indicating that the results are essentially in equilibrium. The effect of the Al content is demonstrated by comparing the Al2CoCrFeNi and AlCoCrFeNi HEA systems. cited_evidence.kind: web:Temperature-dependent ordering within the BCC solid solution
cited_evidence.text: We observe the following trends for AlxCoCrFeNi, for the range 1 < x < 2, summarized in Fig. 7: there is a strongly x-dependent B2-ordering temperature, ranging in the simulations from approximately 1220 °C for x = 1 to 1850 °C for x = 2. For x = 1, this value is close to the temperature where B2 superlattice peaks are first observed (Fig. 4b). These compounds melt near 1300 °C (Fig. 4a, b). Thus, for x = 2, the prediction is that the compound will have strong B2 order on solidification, consistent with our scattering experiments (Fig. 4a). We predict that the system will have weak B2 order on solidification for most compositions in this range. We further predict a weakly x-dependent temperature where the B2 and BCC solid solutions become strongly separated. This unexpectedly sharp transformation occurs very closely to an observed change in the microstructure, using in situ microscopy during heating (Fig. 6b, c), and at a temperature very close to a peak observed through calorimetry for x = 1 (Supplementary Figure S3). decision.trend: Early work on Al‐containing high-entropy alloys documented that alloy composition and thermal history dramatically alter phase constitution without offering a predictive model. Subsequently, approaches (as in PMC6207727) integrated first-principles parameterization into simulation (via Monte Carlo methods) to reproduce key temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolutions. These studies advanced understanding by connecting simulation predictions to observed multiphase behavior, yet they stopped short of isolating, via a controlled experiment, the precise threshold at which the thermodynamic instability (arising from composition) overcomes kinetic barriers in a high-temperature BCC state. In short, the trend has been to move from descriptive phase mapping towards attempts at predictive modeling – but without a direct, controlled test that decouples the proposed driving forces.
decision.unsolved: The central gap is a lack of a single, testable mechanistic explanation that quantitatively links the composition-dependent thermodynamic instability to the onset of phase transformation in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, specifically pinpointing when and how a critical compositional threshold (and attendant accelerated diffusion kinetics) triggers the departure from a BCC state.
decision.lever: Implementing systematic in situ high-temperature annealing experiments combined with real-time X-ray diffraction (or similar structural characterization) to monitor phase-fraction evolution. This setup should involve precisely controlled temperature ramps and hold times to isolate the threshold temperature and time scales at which diffusion overcomes kinetic barriers, along with targeted microanalytical measurements to quantify local compositional fluctuations.
decision.why: Such a controlled-variable strategy provides the means to directly test the hypothesis that a specific thermodynamic threshold (dictated by local compositional instability) activates rapid, diffusion-controlled phase transformation from BCC. This follows naturally from prior simulation-driven insights and addresses the explicit need, defined by previous studies, to decouple and validate the roles of thermodynamic versus kinetic factors in governing phase stability.
